title: When needs outpace provision

blocks.heading: When needs outpace provision
blocks.text: Rapid urban growth can place pressure on housing, water, sanitation, transport and employment where provision does not expand with needs. Problems depend on service capacity, location and access as well as population numbers; residents are not themselves the cause of poor planning or exclusion. In an invented settlement, households increase from 500 to 900 while functioning water points remain at five. Households per point rise from 100 to 180. The additional demand can lengthen queues if supply and use conditions are similar. The ratio identifies pressure, not the measured waiting time or an explanation of why services were not expanded.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Effects on rural areas
blocks.text: Departure can reduce available rural labour or care support, while remittances and new connections can also support rural households. The net effect depends on who leaves, when work is needed, whether earnings are available and whether money or knowledge returns. In a fictional village, several experienced workers leave before planting and remaining households cannot hire replacements. A labour shortage may delay planting and reduce production. In a different case, earnings sent home might finance tools or hired help. Do not assume departure has only a cost or only a benefit.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Housing needs and informal settlements
blocks.text: When affordable housing and serviced land are insufficient, some residents build or occupy housing outside formal planning or tenure arrangements. Informal settlements vary; inadequate infrastructure or insecure access can affect living conditions, but a settlement label does not describe every household. The syllabus term shanty towns refers to a form of low-quality informal housing. Use respectful descriptions of the actual shelter, service and access conditions. In an invented town, rents exceed new workers’ earnings and no serviced low-cost plots are available. Self-built housing near work can meet an immediate shelter need while leaving water and sanitation unresolved.

blocks.heading: Sanitation pressure
blocks.text: Sanitation concerns safe management of human waste, and insufficient capacity can leave waste poorly contained or treated. When demand exceeds functioning provision, contamination of the living environment becomes a greater concern. In a fictional settlement, household numbers rise but toilets and waste-removal capacity do not. Overflowing facilities and uncollected waste show a service gap rather than proof of residents’ habits. A response needs usable facilities, maintenance and a workable disposal route, not construction alone.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Water supply and pollution
blocks.text: Water provision depends on a safe and accessible supply, functioning distribution and management of demand and contamination. A damaged or overloaded system can combine access difficulties with pollution risks where waste reaches the supply. In an invented neighbourhood, households rely on a shared water point beside an overflowing drain, and several supply interruptions force collection from an unprotected alternative. Both reliability and protection matter. More pipe capacity would not by itself address waste reaching the collection area; drainage management alone would not restore missing supply.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Transport and communication
blocks.text: Transport connects residents with work and services, while communication supports access to information and coordination. Growth at poorly connected edges can increase journey time and costs and limit the opportunities residents can actually reach. In a fictional settlement, homes expand beyond a bus route and workers walk far before boarding an already full bus. Frequent late arrivals can threaten access to work even when vacancies exist. A route extension, frequency improvement or better connection should be judged against distance, capacity and affordability rather than road length alone.

blocks.heading: Develop the mechanism
blocks.text: Take a new fictional case: a town adds 200 households but its water points and sanitation capacity are unchanged. Greater demand can lengthen collection queues and overload waste facilities, creating linked access and environmental problems. To explain the effect, use both the increase in demand and the unchanged capacity. Do not invent measured illness rates or queue times. Rural household effects and housing costs are separate mechanisms that also need their own evidence. Topic 7.2 develops the health context; this lesson identifies infrastructure and access pressures.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect causes and responses
blocks.text: Link each observed service or livelihood constraint to the relevant mechanism and affected people; avoid blaming residents or assuming identical experiences.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
